title: Phone permissions and apps from outside the store
body_md:
## A permission is access, not a verdict

A wallpaper app asks to read your contacts, and you hesitate. A map asks where you are, and you tap Allow without a thought. Those instincts are sound, but they are only a start. An app asks for the camera, microphone, location, contacts, photos or notifications because a feature needs them, and the same grant can open far more than the task you had in mind. So put three questions to each request: **which feature is this for, does it need access all the time or only while I’m using it, and what breaks if I say no?** A map needs location for directions; a wallpaper app normally has no use for your contacts. An odd request is a reason to look closer, not proof of malware.

On an iPhone, Settings → Privacy & Security lists apps by type of data, and you can grant or revoke access there. On Android, Settings → Security & privacy/Privacy → Privacy dashboard shows recent use on supported versions and leads on to each app’s permissions. Some apps carry an extra permission or cloud-sharing switch of their own, so changing the OS-level grant may not pull back data that has already been uploaded. Check the app’s account settings too.

Saying no to a legitimate permission may switch off one feature, so try the narrowest option on offer: selected photos, approximate location, access only while using the app. Then reopen the feature and see whether it still works. A valet key starts the engine and leaves the glovebox shut, and that is the size of key to hand out.

## Installing from outside the store is its own decision

On Android, an APK that arrives in a message or on a website skips the normal Play Store route. Google Play Protect scans apps from other sources too, but a clean scan is no guarantee. If anything asks you to turn scanning off, grant Accessibility, read your notifications or install yet another package, stop. Those powers can let an app watch sensitive screens or act on them. Get the app from the publisher’s official channel, one you find yourself, and work out why it is being distributed this way. If the source or the need is unclear, put the installation off. Do not follow a link sent by someone who rang you out of the blue.

On iPhone, the rules for installing apps from outside the App Store differ by region and OS version. Do not assume every iPhone can install arbitrary apps, or that the App Store or any alternative store has kept every malicious app out. Device-management profiles and enterprise distribution call for the same independent check. And if your work or school manages the phone, ask its administrator before you remove a control it requires.

## A review you can repeat

Begin with the grants that carry the most weight: contacts, notification access, accessibility, precise or background location, microphone, camera and the full photo library. For each app, work out the real feature and the publisher, shrink the grant where you can, then test the feature. Uninstall an app you no longer need, and remove its account access separately if it has any. Keep the OS and your apps updated.

If you have already installed a suspicious package, stop using it. Remove its permissions and then the app itself through system settings, run Play Protect if you are on Android, and review the accounts you used on that phone from a trusted device. If the app held powerful device-control access, you may need a reset or help from the provider. The exact recovery depends on the device.

widget_config.goal: Go through one app permission by permission, match each to a feature it really has, and work out whether installing anything from outside the store is justified.
widget_config.today_action: Open the system’s permission list. Look at one app you no longer use and one that handles your photos or messages, and revoke whatever access has no current purpose. On Android, also check that Play Protect is on.
widget_config.scope: General Android and iOS guidance as of 2026-10-20. Menu names and alternative app distribution vary by OS, device, country and store policy. The people and parcels in the examples are invented. Permissions and store review lower the risk, but neither certifies an app.

blocks.title: The parcel that needs an APK
blocks.situation: A text from a courier firm says Mira’s parcel will be lost unless she installs “ParcelTrack.apk” and enables notification access. The link is not real.
blocks.analysis: Notification access has nothing to do with looking at a parcel, and it can reveal verification messages. Mira checks her orders in the retailer app she already uses and asks the courier through its known channel. She does not install the file. A real delivery could still exist, so she verifies the order rather than dismissing it.

blocks.title: A scan button asks for the camera
blocks.situation: A banking app Leon already uses asks for the camera only when he taps “scan document,” and it offers limited photo selection as well.
blocks.analysis: The timing and the feature make camera access plausible. Leon allows it while using the app, checks that the document goes to the bank’s expected workflow, and revokes the access later if he is not using it. A permission alone does not prove that the app or its destination is genuine.

blocks.title: Setting up a relative’s phone
blocks.setup: An invented practice: a relative wants a parcel tracker and an app for scanning photos. No real package, code or account data is entered.

steps.prompt: A text offers a parcel-tracker APK and says Play Protect has to be switched off first. What is your first move?

choices.text: Open the retailer’s app you already have, or type its address in yourself.
choices.consequence: You can check the order without letting a stranger install anything.
choices.explanation: Going there yourself separates the real service from the message.

choices.text: Switch off Play Protect for a minute, install the APK, then switch it back on.
choices.consequence: The package may gain powerful access before you have checked who published it.
choices.explanation: A request to switch off a safeguard is reason enough to stop, whatever the message promises.

steps.prompt: A scanner app you know asks for all your photos when you need one image.

choices.consequence: Photos that have nothing to do with the scan become reachable by the app.
choices.explanation: The convenient default is wider than a one-image job.

choices.text: Use selected-photo access if it is offered, then test the scan.
choices.consequence: The feature works, with less of your library exposed.
choices.explanation: Grant the minimum the current task needs.

steps.prompt: The scanner now asks for the microphone, though you only scan paper.

choices.text: Decline and see whether scanning still works; look into any voice feature later.
choices.consequence: Scanning can carry on if it never needed audio.
choices.explanation: A permission should follow a feature, not the mere appearance of a prompt.

choices.text: Allow it. The app comes from a store.
choices.consequence: Store review neither explains this grant nor limits it.
choices.explanation: Where an app came from is one signal, not grounds to approve every request.

steps.prompt: Now look at a different tracker app your relative installed last week, before today’s message. It already has notification access, which a tracker has no use for, and it is not the APK from step 1. What next?

choices.text: Leave it. Nothing bad has visibly happened.
choices.consequence: The app keeps receiving every future notification.
choices.explanation: A quiet phone does not make unneeded access safe.

choices.text: Revoke the access, uninstall the suspect app, and review the affected accounts from a trusted device.
choices.consequence: The exposure stops, and you can look into what happened.
choices.explanation: Revoking now cannot undo earlier access, which is why the accounts need review.

blocks.debrief: Play the four decisions again with three habits in mind: check the publisher independently, grant the smallest permission that works, and investigate past access as a separate question.

blocks.title: Try it on a new app

questions.prompt: A map you know asks for location only when you start a route. What is the best response?

choices.text: Allow while using the app, and review it later.
choices.explanation: The permission matches the feature without a standing background grant.

choices.text: Refuse location to every app, always.
choices.explanation: That switches off a legitimate route feature for no reason.

choices.text: Give precise location, background included, forever.
choices.explanation: That is far more than one trip needs.

questions.prompt: You revoke contacts access and an app’s address-book feature gets worse. What does that prove?

choices.explanation: A feature that stops working says nothing about anyone’s intent.

choices.text: Only that the feature may need contacts. Look at what it does and who publishes the app.
choices.explanation: Refusing a legitimate permission can cost you a feature, which makes the loss a poor test for malware.

questions.prompt: Play Protect finds nothing wrong with an unknown APK. What follows?

choices.text: Keep checking the publisher and the need on your own; a scan covers only part of the picture.
choices.explanation: Scans can miss behavior that is new or built to hide.

choices.text: Granting it Accessibility must now be safe.
choices.explanation: A clean scan does not certify an app for powerful access.

questions.prompt: After you uninstall an app, what may still need attention?

choices.text: Its cloud account access and the data already uploaded.
choices.explanation: Uninstalling ends local use of the app but cannot automatically erase remote copies.
